W5. Single-cell RNA-seq — Technology, QC, Clustering

Author

Eunji Ha

Published

October 9, 2026

Note🎯 Learning objectives

By the end of this chapter you should be able to:

  • Say what single cell answers that bulk structurally cannot — and when bulk is still the better buy
  • Choose between droplet and plate-based protocols, and ⚠️ between cells and nuclei
  • ⚠️ Explain why dissociation changes the composition you measure
  • Explain what a UMI is, and why the count matrix is mostly zeros
  • ⚠️ Read a knee plot and a QC scatter, and name the population each threshold deletes
  • Explain how a doublet detector works — and which doublets no detector can see
  • ⚠️ Read a UMAP responsibly — and say what its distances do and do not mean
  • ⚠️ Say which version of the matrix — raw, normalised, scaled, batch-corrected — each step should use
  • ⚠️ Explain why per-cell differential expression across conditions is invalid, and what pseudobulk does instead

🤔 Motivating question

Your bulk RNA-seq shows a clean two-fold increase, p = 0.001. Is that every cell changing a little, 5% of cells changing enormously, or no cell changing at all?

1. What Bulk Cannot See 🔬

1) three biologies in a single number

① A general modest response: the case everyone implicitly assumes, and the least interesting
② A rare responsive subpopulation: usually the interesting one. In bulk it is diluted by the cells doing nothing, and often falls below significance entirely
③ A change in composition: not any novel cell types. There are simply more of one cell type

⚠️ ③ deserves attention because it is common in inflamed, fibrotic or infiltrated tissue — exactly the tissue clinicians study — and it is routinely written up as if it were ①.

2) When single cell is worth it

Single cell is expensive –> Be specific! Bulk can be enough in many cases

✅ Single cell is right for:

  • Discovering or characterising populations, including rare ones
  • Composition — which cell types shifted in disease
  • Cell-type-specific effects — a gene up in one cell type and down in another, invisible in bulk
  • Continuous states — activation, exhaustion, differentiation, where discrete labels fail

✅ Bulk is still right for:

  • A well-defined comparison in a homogeneous system (cell line, sorted population)
  • Deep transcript-level work — isoforms, splicing, low-expression genes
  • Large cohorts — n = 200 patients, where 200 single-cell runs is unaffordable
TipSorting first is badly underrated

Already know which cell type you care about?

→ FACS-sort it and run deep bulk RNA-seq. Often cheaper, deeper, and statistically cleaner than a whole-tissue single-cell experiment — and you can afford far more patients, which (§5) is where your power actually comes from.

💡 “We did single cell” is not by itself a stronger design. Sometimes it is a more expensive way to be underpowered.

2. Decisions Made Before the Machine 🤔

1) The platform trade-off

Every platform buys cells with depth, or depth with cells.

Platform Cells Depth When
Droplet (10x) 10³–10⁵ a few thousand genes/cell, 3′ or 5′ end only the current default
Plate (Smart-seq3) 10² full-length, deep isoforms, very sensitive detection
Combinatorial (sci-, SPLiT-seq) 10⁶ very shallow whole-organism atlases

2) 3′ vs. 5′ (for droplet kits)

one end of each transcript, not the full length — enough to count genes, not to see isoforms.

  • ✅ Most single-cell data is 3′, including most public atlases. 5′ is the choice when you need clonotypes: T/B cells, tumour immunology, autoimmunity, vaccine responses
  • ⚠️ For gene counting the two are broadly similar, but not interchangeable within one comparison — 3′ and 5′ samples mixed in one study are a batch effect by design
  • 💡 For fixed or FFPE samples there is a third route: probe-based kits (10x Flex) that hybridise probes instead of capturing the poly(A) tail
  • The bead drawn in §3.2 is a 5′ bead — note the TSO at its end

3) Cells vs nuclei

⚠️ Decided at collection, not at analysis
scRNA-seq needs fresh, viable tissue dissociated into intact cells

scRNA-seq snRNA-seq
Frozen / archived tissue ❌ needs fresh ✅
Large or fragile cells (neurons, adipocytes, myofibres, cardiomyocytes) ❌ lost in dissociation ✅
Dissociation stress response ⚠️ yes — FOS, JUN, heat-shock genes induced by the protocol ✅ minimal
Cytoplasmic transcripts ✅ captured ❌ missed
Intronic reads low high — nuclei are rich in unspliced pre-mRNA
WarningTwo consequences worth carrying into a design meeting
  • ⚠️ Immediate-early genes are the classic false positive. A cluster defined by FOS, JUN and EGR1 is very often a dissociation artifact, not an “activated” state. If one condition sat on the bench longer, it will look more activated
  • ⚠️ Depletion claims need scrutiny. “Cell type X is depleted in disease” and “cell type X is harder to release from diseased tissue” produce identical data

→ ✅ Mitigations: dissociate at low temperature with cold-active protease, keep the protocol identical across conditions, and — best — use nuclei when the tissue allows it.

4) considerations for a study design

⚠️ Your unit of replication is the donor. Everything in §5 follows from this, and it should shape the budget before it shapes the analysis.

💡 Given a fixed budget: more donors, fewer cells each beats fewer donors, more cells each for almost any question that compares conditions.

3. Data pre-processing 🧮

1) the standard pipeline: from Droplets to a Matrix

so many steps😟? –> the more steps, the more errors propagate …😵‍💫

2) capturing a single-cell

① two tags: Barcodes and UMIs

  • Cell barcode — identical on every oligo of one bead → every molecule captured in that droplet is tagged “from this cell”
  • UMI (unique molecular identifier) — random, different on every oligo → tags each original mRNA molecule before amplification

✅ The matrix counts molecules, not reads — PCR duplicates and amplification bias are removed
⚠️ What UMIs cannot fix: a molecule that was never captured gets no UMI at all. Hence the zeros below

Warningsparsity: why the matrix is over 90% zeros

A droplet experiment detects roughly 1,000–5,000 genes per cell, out of ~20,000.
Zero count means:

  • Biological zero — the gene really is not expressed in that cell
  • Technical zero (dropout) — the transcript was there and was not captured. Droplet capture efficiency is ~10–30%

② cell calling

Which barcodes are cells, and which are empty droplets?

  • Droplets. Cells are loaded dilute on purpose
  • Barcode rank plot (knee plot). Rank every barcode by total UMI count and plot on log–log axes:
  • ① High plateau — real cells
  • ② Steep drop (the knee) — the transition
  • ③ Long low tail — empty droplets carrying only ambient RNA

⚠️ A hard cut at the knee deletes real cells that simply have little RNA — small or quiescent cells, neutrophils. They sit exactly in the transition zone.

✅ EmptyDrops (Cell Ranger ≥ 3 uses a version of it) asks a better question: not “is the total high?” but “is this barcode’s profile different from the ambient profile?” A small cell with a distinct profile is kept even though its total is low.

💡 Cell Ranger writes two matrices: filtered_feature_bc_matrix (called cells) and raw_feature_bc_matrix (every barcode). Keep the raw one — ambient-RNA correction needs the empty droplets.

③ removal of ambient RNA

Cells that burst during dissociation and loading release their mRNA into the suspension. This “soup” is captured in every droplet, so every cell’s profile = its own RNA + a little soup.

  • What it looks like — markers of the most abundant or most fragile cell type at low level in every cluster: haemoglobin genes in every cell of a bloody sample, ALB in the immune cells of a liver
  • Why it matters — false co-expression, blurred cluster boundaries, and ⚠️ false DE when one condition releases more soup (diseased, necrotic tissue usually does)

⚠️ every droplet-based protocol has it, and snRNA-seq the most (isolating nuclei lyses every cell)

💡 Well-based platforms (BD Rhapsody, plate-based Smart-seq) usually skip this step. Cells settle or are sorted into separate wells carrying little of the surrounding buffer, so far less soup is captured than in a droplet, which seals the buffer in with the cell. ⚠️ Less is not zero — the same symptom (one cell type’s markers everywhere) still means contamination.

Tool Input Idea
SoupX raw + filtered matrix, clusters Estimates the soup from empty droplets, then subtracts a contamination fraction
CellBender raw matrix Generative model that calls cells and removes ambient RNA in one step; GPU recommended
DecontX filtered matrix (raw optional) Bayesian; usable when the empty droplets were not kept

✅ Run it before QC and clustering, on each sample separately — the corrected counts are the input to everything below.

3) data QC: your own cutoffs

① low-quality QC

Three numbers per cell:

Metric Seurat / scanpy Too low → Too high →
Total UMIs nCount_RNA / total_counts empty droplet, debris, broken cell doublet — or a large, active cell
Genes detected nFeature_RNA / n_genes_by_counts as above as above
Mitochondrial % percent.mt / pct_counts_mt — dying cell — or a mitochondria-rich one

Why a high mito fraction means a dying cell: when the membrane breaks, cytoplasmic mRNA leaks out, but transcripts inside mitochondria are protected by the mitochondrial membrane and stay. The fraction rises — not because the cell made more.

⚠️ Read them jointly. High mito and few genes = broken cell. High mito with a normal gene count may be a genuinely mitochondria-rich cell (cardiomyocyte, hepatocyte, renal tubule)
⚠️ snRNA-seq: nuclei contain no mitochondria, so mito reads should be near zero. Any real fraction is cytoplasmic or ambient contamination → a much stricter cut

✅ Data-driven cutoffs: flag cells more than k median absolute deviations (MADs) from the median (scater::isOutlier; k = 3 strict … 5 permissive) — the threshold adapts to each sample
✅ Per sample, always. A more deeply sequenced sample shifts all three distributions

ImportantEvery threshold needs its rationale
  • A mito cutoff of 5% is conventional — and wrong for cardiomyocytes, which are genuinely mitochondria-rich. need to set your data-specific cutoffs
  • min.features = 500 removes debris — and also platelets, some granulocytes, and any small low-RNA cell
  • An upper nFeature cutoff removes doublets — and also genuinely large, transcriptionally active cells

✅ Plot the distribution, look at what sits outside your proposed cut → decide your own thresholds

② doublets

Two cells in one droplet share a barcode and look like one cell with a hybrid profile. The rate rises with loading: ~0.8% per 1,000 cells recovered on standard 10x — 10,000 cells → ~8% doublets.

Heterotypic Homotypic
Made of two different cell types (T cell + monocyte) two cells of the same type
Looks like markers of both types; a fake “intermediate” cluster or a bridge between clusters one cell with ~2× the counts
Detectable from expression ✅ yes ❌ almost never
Damage ⚠️ invented cell types and transitions mild

The core idea: we never see which barcodes are doublets — but we can make doublets, and then ask which real cells look like them.

DoubletFinder — the logic in four steps

  1. Simulate — make artificial doublets by averaging the profiles of random pairs of real cells (pN, default 25% of the merged data)
  2. Embed together — real + artificial cells → normalise, HVGs, PCA
  3. Count fake neighbours — for each real cell, pANN = the proportion of artificial doublets among its nearest neighbours. A real doublet sits among the fakes → high pANN
  4. Threshold — rank by pANN and call the top n as doublets, where n = expected rate × cells, reduced by the homotypic fraction it cannot see (modelHomotypic())

The one parameter that matters is pK, the neighbourhood size. DoubletFinder sweeps it and keeps the value at which pANN is most bimodal — singlets low, doublets high — scored by BCmvn (mean–variance-normalised bimodality coefficient).

💡 A clearly bimodal pANN distribution is your evidence that the call works. A unimodal one means doublets are not separable at that neighbourhood size.

library(DoubletFinder)

# one sample at a time, after permissive QC, normalisation, PCA and a rough clustering
sweep <- paramSweep(seu, PCs = 1:10, sct = FALSE)
bcmvn <- find.pK(summarizeSweep(sweep, GT = FALSE))
pK    <- as.numeric(as.character(bcmvn$pK[which.max(bcmvn$BCmetric)]))

homotypic <- modelHomotypic(seu$seurat_clusters)    # share of same-type doublets
rate      <- 0.008 * ncol(seu) / 1000               # ~0.8% per 1,000 cells (10x)
nExp      <- round(rate * ncol(seu) * (1 - homotypic))

seu <- doubletFinder(seu, PCs = 1:10, pN = 0.25, pK = pK, nExp = nExp, sct = FALSE)
# → new metadata columns pANN_* and DF.classifications_* (Singlet / Doublet)

scDblFinder — what is different?

Same core idea (artificial doublets, and where real cells sit among them), different machinery:

DoubletFinder scDblFinder
Artificial doublets random pairs random, or between clusters — focused on the heterotypic ones that matter
Score one statistic (pANN) at one neighbourhood size gradient-boosted classifier on kNN features at several sizes + library size, detected genes, co-expression; retrained iteratively
Parameters pK sweep; expected n set by hand threshold set automatically from the expected rate and misclassification
Multiple samples run each sample yourself samples = argument
Speed slow (the pK sweep) fast

DoubletFinder was the most accurate method in the first large independent benchmark (Xi & Li 2021). scDblFinder, released later, matched or beat it on the same datasets (Germain et al. 2021) and is now a common default — it is the tool in the pipeline figure.

library(scDblFinder)
sce <- scDblFinder(as.SingleCellExperiment(seu), samples = "sample_id")
seu$doublet <- sce$scDblFinder.class                # "singlet" / "doublet"
WarningRules for any doublet detector

⚠️ One sample (capture) at a time. Doublets form only within a capture; artificial doublets between two patients describe cells that cannot exist
⚠️ Homotypic doublets survive every expression-based method. Accept a residual
⚠️ Do it before you interpret clusters. A doublet cluster sits between its two parents and is easily named a transitional state
💡 Design beats algorithms. Pool donors in one lane and demultiplex by genotype (demuxlet, souporcell, vireo) or by hashtag antibodies → every between-donor doublet is identified directly, and you can load more cells per lane

③ Recap

Problem What it looks like What to do
Empty droplets Low-UMI barcodes below the knee EmptyDrops, not a hard cutoff
Ambient RNA Markers of abundant cell types appearing everywhere SoupX, CellBender, DecontX
Doublets High UMI and high gene count; two incompatible marker sets scDblFinder, DoubletFinder; ~0.8% per 1,000 cells recovered
Dying cells High mitochondrial fraction, low gene count Threshold on mito %, tissue-specifically
TipWhich comes first — doublets or QC?

The two tools’ own documentation points in opposite directions:

  • DoubletFinder: remove low-quality clusters first — they distort the artificial doublets and the PCA
  • scDblFinder: find doublets before stringent QC — the expected rate is computed from the cells you hand it, and a doublet of one good and one bad cell is recognisable only while the bad one is still in the data

✅ The order that reconciles them — ① then ② above, as in the pipeline figure:

  1. Primary QC, permissive — remove only obvious junk: near-empty barcodes, extreme mito
  2. Doublet detection, per sample
  3. Final thresholds, data-driven (MADs)
  4. Secondary QC after clustering — drop whole clusters defined by mito or stress genes, or by two incompatible marker sets (§4.4)

💡 Either order is defensible if you state it. What is not: an upper nFeature cutoff as your only doublet filter.

4) dimension reduction

After QC: thousands of cells × ~20,000 genes, mostly zeros

① normalization & scaling

Step What it does Why Seurat
Normalise divide by the cell’s total UMIs, × 10,000, then log(1 + x) capture efficiency differs several-fold between cells for purely technical reasons; the log tames a few huge values NormalizeData()
Select HVGs keep ~2,000 genes whose variance exceeds what their mean predicts most genes are flat or noise; HVGs carry the cell-type signal FindVariableFeatures()
Scale per gene: subtract the mean, divide by the SD so a highly expressed gene does not dominate PCA simply by being large ScaleData()
Note

💡 Alternatives: SCTransform (Pearson residuals from a regularised negative binomial model — all three steps in one) and scran pooled size factors. A large benchmark found the plain shifted log + PCA does as well as or better than the sophisticated options (Ahlmann-Eltze & Huber 2023)
⚠️ ScaleData(vars.to.regress = ...) can regress out mito %, depth or cell-cycle score. Use sparingly: if the “nuisance” is correlated with biology — cycling cells in a proliferative disease — you regress out the biology too
⚠️ Three versions of the same matrix now sit side by side. §5.1 depends on knowing which is which:

  • counts — raw UMIs
  • data — log-normalised
  • scale.data — z-scores, HVGs only

② PCA: dimension reduction

2,000 HVGs → 10–50 principal components. Each PC is a weighted combination of genes that move together — a program, not a gene.

  • Denoising — single genes are noisy; correlated programs are not. Top PCs carry biology, later ones mostly noise
  • Speed — everything downstream (neighbours, clustering, UMAP, batch correction) runs on PCs, not genes
  • How many? ElbowPlot() — where the variance explained flattens. Results are fairly stable across 10–50; err high rather than low, since a rare population can live in PC 25

✅ Check what drives the top PCs. If PC1 tracks nCount_RNA or percent.mt, your main axis of variation is technical → back to QC. VizDimLoadings() shows the genes
💡 PCA is linear and its distances are meaningful — unlike UMAP (§4.3). PC space is where the analysis actually happens; UMAP is only how we look at it.

③ batch correction

With several samples, cells often group by donor or batch before cell type. Correction works on the embedding, not on the counts:

  • Harmony — iteratively adjusts the PCs
  • scVI — learns a new latent space from raw counts, with batch as a covariate
  • Seurat CCA / RPCA — anchors matched cells between datasets

→ for neighbours, clustering and UMAP

✅ Check first whether you need it. Colour the uncorrected UMAP by sample. If cell types already mix across samples, skip it
⚠️ Corrected values are for grouping cells, not for testing genes. DE goes back to raw counts, with donor in the model (§5.1)
⚠️ Over-correction can erase a disease-specific state → 🔗 W6 §1

NoteThe VI universe — one engine, many models

scVI is the first member of a family (the scvi-tools library). All share one engine:

  • A variational autoencoder (VAE) — a neural network compresses each cell’s raw counts into ~10–30 latent numbers, and a decoder reconstructs the counts with a negative binomial model
  • Batch is handed to the decoder as an input, so the latent space does not have to encode it — that is the integration
  • Change the likelihood or add a modality → a new model
Model Data Used for In this course
scVI scRNA-seq integration, denoised expression, DE here, W6
scANVI scRNA-seq + some cell-type labels label transfer, annotation §4.4
scArches new data + a trained reference model mapping a query onto an atlas without retraining §4.4
totalVI CITE-seq (RNA + surface protein) joint RNA–protein analysis; removes antibody background
PeakVI scATAC-seq chromatin accessibility: integration, differential accessibility
MultiVI multiome (RNA + ATAC), paired or not integrating multiome with single-modality data W11
DestVI spatial spots + scRNA reference deconvolution, including continuous states within a cell type W8
veloVI spliced / unspliced counts RNA velocity with uncertainty W6
contrastiveVI perturbed vs control cells separating treatment-specific from shared variation
MrVI many samples / donors sample-level (donor) differences in large cohorts
  • 💡 Practical: all of them want raw counts (keep the counts layer), run in Python (scvi-tools; a GPU helps), and reach R via reticulate or an exported .h5ad
  • ⚠️ Same caution as any integration: the latent space is for grouping cells. A model told to remove “batch” also removes any biology confounded with batch (W6 §1)

4. Finding Cell Types 🗺️

1) neighbors for grouping cells

Clustering and UMAP never see genes. They see a graph of which cells are near which, built in PC space.

  • Neighbours — for each cell, the k cells closest to it in PC space (Euclidean distance on the top PCs)
  • kNN graph — cells are nodes; each cell is linked to its k neighbours. Seurat then reweights each link by how many neighbours the two cells share (SNN graph), which damps outliers
  • Why a graph — cell populations are rarely round blobs. A graph follows the shape of the data, including elongated, branching and continuous populations, and scales to millions of cells

⚠️ “kNN clustering” is a misnomer. kNN only builds the graph; clustering (next) cuts it into communities. Nor is it k-means, which needs the number of clusters in advance and assumes round clusters.

⚠️ k sets the scale (k.param = 20 in Seurat, n_neighbors = 15 in scanpy). Small k → fine local structure, more fragments. Large k → a smoother graph, and a population with fewer cells than k cannot be its own neighbourhood — its members are forced to link outside it.

2) clustering

① leiden vs. louvain

Concept only — recognise the names and know what they optimise; no need to implement them.

  • Both are community detection: cut the graph into groups whose cells are more densely linked to each other than chance would predict (maximising modularity)
  • Louvain (2008) — greedily move each cell into the neighbouring community that most improves modularity; collapse each community into one node; repeat
  • ⚠️ Known flaw: it can return badly connected or even disconnected communities — a “cluster” whose pieces are not linked in the graph
  • Leiden (2019) — adds a refinement step that guarantees every community is internally connected; also faster
  • Defaults: scanpy → Leiden. Seurat FindClusters() → Louvain (algorithm = 1); Leiden is algorithm = 4

💡 For the biology, the choice rarely changes the conclusion. Resolution does — report both.

② resolution

key parameter for clustering: resolution

Resolution is a term inside the modularity score: higher values reward smaller communities → more clusters.

⚠️ the best resolution is up to you…

  • Check clusters against marker genes and known biology, not against a score
  • Check stability: does the cluster survive a different resolution, a different seed, a subsampled dataset?
  • Ask whether a “new” cluster at higher resolution has genuinely distinct markers, or just gradations of the same ones
NoteA cluster is not a cell type

Clusters can equally reflect:

  • cell state (activated vs resting)
  • cell-cycle phase
  • stress response (§2.3)
  • ambient contamination
  • donor identity

⚠️ Naming a cluster after its top marker gene and treating it as a cell type is how the literature accumulates cell types that do not exist.

3) UMAP

a non-linear projection of tens of dimensions into two. It preserves local neighbourhoods reasonably and global structure badly.

Why UMAP became the default for complex tissue:

  • It lays out the same kNN graph as clustering (§4.1) — so its islands usually agree with your clusters
  • Strong pull between neighbours → compact islands with clear gaps, where t-SNE spreads groups evenly over a round cloud
  • It starts from the graph’s own (spectral) layout, not random positions → related populations tend to land near each other, and reruns look alike
  • Fast — millions of cells, where t-SNE is slow

⚠️ The t-distribution is not what makes t-SNE look round — its heavy tail is what lets t-SNE open gaps at all. The rounder, looser look comes from a weaker pull between neighbours, and the arbitrary arrangement from the random start. Start t-SNE from PCA and strengthen the pull, and it looks UMAP-like.

NoteWhat a UMAP does not tell you

❌ Distances between clusters are not meaningful. Two clusters far apart are not necessarily more different than two that are close
❌ Cluster areas are not meaningful. Size reflects the embedding, not cell number
❌ Apparent bridges are not trajectories. A thin connection may be doublets, ambient RNA, or a parameter artifact
⚠️ The layout changes with parameters and random seed. n_neighbors and min_dist

→ A UMAP is a picture of your data, not a measurement of it. Any claim that matters should be supported by a number computed in the high-dimensional space.

Note

PCA, t-SNE, UMAP — and the newer ones

Method Year Preserves Where you see it
PCA 1901 global, linear structure; distances meaningful input to everything downstream; too crude to view clusters
t-SNE 2008 local neighbourhoods; global layout arbitrary the standard before UMAP; slower
UMAP 2018 local neighbourhoods, some global structure; fast the current default
PHATE 2019 continuous transitions and branches development, differentiation
densMAP 2021 also local density — a homogeneous population stays tight, a heterogeneous one spreads out when “how variable is this population” matters
PaCMAP 2021 a balance of local and global structure general-purpose; less common in single-cell papers so far

💡 UMAP’s reputation for better global structure than t-SNE comes mostly from its initialisation, not the algorithm; t-SNE started from PCA does about as well (Kobak & Linderman 2021)

⚠️ Every one of them is still a 2D picture. The newer methods trade one distortion for another; none turns 2D distance into a measurement (Chari & Pachter 2023)

4) Annotation

  • Marker-based — check known markers per cluster.
    ✅ Transparent.
    ⚠️ Circular: you find the cell types you looked for
  • Reference-based — map onto an annotated atlas (Azimuth, SingleR, scANVI).
    ✅ Fast and consistent.
    ⚠️ Inherits the reference’s vocabulary and cannot name anything the reference lacks

💡 Use both. Disagreements between them are the informative part — that is where a genuinely novel or genuinely artifactual population sits.

5. Statistics (DEG analysis) 📊

1) values to use

By now each cell carries several versions of its expression (§3.4). Testing on the wrong one is a common and silent error.

Value Where ✅ Use for ❌ Not for
Raw UMI counts
(or ambient-corrected)		 counts layer (Seurat), .layers["counts"] (scanpy) pseudobulk DE (§5.3), any count model comparing cells directly (depth differs)
Log-normalised data layer (Seurat), .X after normalize_total + log1p (scanpy) cluster markers within one dataset (§5.2), feature plots condition comparisons with cells as n
Scaled (z-scores) scale.data layer (Seurat), .X after sc.pp.scale (scanpy) PCA, heatmaps any DE
Batch-corrected
(from Harmony / scVI)		 reductions, e.g. harmony (Seurat), .obsm["X_pca_harmony"], .obsm["X_scVI"] (scanpy) neighbours, clustering, UMAP any DE
scVI normalised / denoised expression get_normalized_expression() output, usually stored in .layers (scvi-tools) visualisation; scVI’s own DE standard tests that assume observed counts
Tip

⚠️ scanpy gotcha: normalize_total, log1p and scale overwrite .X in place. Copy the raw counts into .layers["counts"] before normalising — otherwise they are gone, and pseudobulk has nothing to sum.

Re-normalise after subsetting one cell type?

  • For sub-clustering — partly, yes. Re-run HVG selection, scaling and PCA on the subset: the HVGs of the whole tissue mostly separate cell types from each other, not states within one type
  • Log-normalisation itself — no. It is computed per cell, so subsetting does not change it
  • For DE — not relevant. Pseudobulk starts from raw counts, and DESeq2/edgeR normalise across pseudo-samples themselves

⚠️ Exception: SCTransform residuals depend on the data they were fitted on. With several SCT models (merged samples), run PrepSCTFindMarkers() before testing

2) per-cell tests

ImportantCells from one donor are not independent samples

A Wilcoxon test across 5,400 cells from 6 donors treats those cells as 5,400 independent observations. They are not — cells from the same person share that person’s genetics, environment, medication, batch and processing.

The consequence:

  • p-values inflated by many orders of magnitude
  • add cells → the p-value shrinks indefinitely
  • → you are measuring how many cells you loaded, not how many people you studied

⚠️ Seurat’s default FindMarkers behaves this way.

  • ✅ Appropriate for identifying cluster markers within one dataset — a descriptive task
  • ❌ Not appropriate for comparing conditions

3) Pseudobulk

for each donor × cell type, sum the counts across cells.

You now have a small matrix of pseudo-samples — analyse it with DESeq2 or edgeR exactly as in last semester’s bulk workflow.

library(Seurat); library(DESeq2); library(tidyverse)

pb <- AggregateExpression(seurat,
                          group.by = c("cell_type", "sample_id"),
                          assays   = "RNA")$RNA

# then, per cell type, a completely ordinary DESeq2 run
  • Benchmarks consistently find pseudobulk controls false positives far better than per-cell tests
  • Mixed models with a donor random effect are a reasonable alternative — more power retained, more computation

4) Differential abundance is compositional

Often the interesting result is not that a cell type changed its expression, but that there is more or less of it.

⚠️ Proportions are compositional — one cell type expands and every other proportion falls by arithmetic alone, with no biology behind it (multivariate).

  • ✅ Methods that handle this: scCODA, miloR, propeller, Dirichlet-multinomial models
  • ❌ A χ² test on cell counts is not valid
  • ⚠️ And before believing any abundance result, return to §2.3: is this composition, or is this dissociation?

6. Hands-On 💻

1) No code: does the atlas already answer it?

CELLxGENE → search a gene from your specialty.

  • ① Which cell types express it, in which tissues?
  • ② Is the expression broad, or confined to one population?
  • ③ Find a dataset in your disease area. How many donors does it have — not how many cells?
  • ④ 💡 If the atlas already answers “which cell type expresses my gene”, you have saved a grant

2) The pipeline, end to end

library(Seurat); library(SeuratData); library(tidyverse)

InstallData("pbmc3k"); data("pbmc3k")
pbmc <- pbmc3k

pbmc[["percent.mt"]] <- PercentageFeatureSet(pbmc, pattern = "^MT-")

# ⚠️ LOOK before you cut
VlnPlot(pbmc, c("nFeature_RNA", "nCount_RNA", "percent.mt"), ncol = 3, pt.size = 0)

pbmc <- subset(pbmc, nFeature_RNA > 200 & nFeature_RNA < 2500 & percent.mt < 5)

pbmc <- NormalizeData(pbmc) |>
  FindVariableFeatures(nfeatures = 2000) |>
  ScaleData() |>
  RunPCA(verbose = FALSE)

ElbowPlot(pbmc, ndims = 30)

pbmc <- FindNeighbors(pbmc, dims = 1:10) |>
  FindClusters(resolution = 0.5) |>
  RunUMAP(dims = 1:10)

DimPlot(pbmc, label = TRUE)

3) ✅ Change one thing

# ① How many cells did each threshold remove, and which ones?
table(pbmc3k$seurat_annotations[pbmc3k$percent.mt >= 5])   # who did the mito cut delete?

# ② Re-cluster at three resolutions and count
for (r in c(0.2, 0.5, 1.2)) {
  pbmc <- FindClusters(pbmc, resolution = r, verbose = FALSE)
  cat("resolution", r, "→", nlevels(pbmc$seurat_clusters), "clusters\n")
}

# ③ Re-run UMAP with a different seed and compare the picture
pbmc <- RunUMAP(pbmc, dims = 1:10, seed.use = 99)
DimPlot(pbmc, label = TRUE)

4) Save for next week

saveRDS(pbmc, here::here("analysis", "5_pbmc_annotated.rds"))

📝 Summary

  • One bulk fold change is compatible with a uniform shift, a rare responsive subpopulation, or a pure composition change
  • ✅ Sorting plus deep bulk on many patients often beats whole-tissue single cell on few
  • ⚠️ Fresh or frozen is decided at collection and fixes scRNA-seq vs snRNA-seq permanently
  • ⚠️ Dissociation induces stress genes and destroys cells selectively. FOS/JUN clusters are usually artifacts; depletion claims need scrutiny
  • UMIs count molecules, not reads. The matrix is >90% zeros and a single zero means little
  • Cell calling and ambient-RNA removal need the raw matrix, empty droplets included — keep it
  • ⚠️ Doublet detection runs per sample; homotypic doublets are invisible to every expression-based method
  • ⚠️ Every QC threshold deletes a real population — mito 5% removes cardiomyocytes, min.features 500 removes platelets
  • The kNN graph in PC space drives both clustering and UMAP. Leiden vs Louvain matters far less than resolution
  • ❌ UMAP distances, cluster areas and bridges are not interpretable
  • ⚠️ Clustering resolution is arbitrary. Check markers and stability, and report the value you used
  • ⚠️ Scaled and batch-corrected values are for grouping cells, never for DE — testing goes back to raw counts
  • ⚠️ Per-cell differential expression across conditions is invalid. Use pseudobulk. Your n is the number of donors
  • ⚠️ Cell-type proportions are compositional — χ² on cell counts is not valid

🔑 Key terms

Term One-line meaning
Cell barcode Sequence identifying which droplet a read came from
UMI Tag marking one original mRNA molecule
Dropout An expressed transcript that was not captured — a technical zero
Knee plot (barcode rank plot) Ranked UMI counts, used to separate cells from empty droplets
Cell calling Deciding which barcodes are cells and which are empty droplets
Ambient RNA Free-floating RNA contaminating every droplet
Doublet Two cells captured in one droplet
Homotypic / heterotypic doublet Same-type pair (nearly undetectable) / different-type pair (hybrid profile)
pANN DoubletFinder’s score: proportion of artificial doublets among a cell’s nearest neighbours
MAD Median absolute deviation — basis for per-sample, data-driven QC cutoffs
snRNA-seq Profiling nuclei rather than whole cells
Dissociation artifact Gene expression induced by the protocol, not the biology
Log-normalisation Scale each cell to the same total, then take log(1 + x)
HVG Highly variable genes selected before PCA
Batch correction Aligning samples in the embedding so cells group by type, not by batch
kNN / SNN graph Each cell linked to its nearest (or shared) neighbours in PC space
UMAP / t-SNE Non-linear 2D embeddings — for visualisation only
Leiden / Louvain Graph-based community detection on the kNN graph; Leiden guarantees connected clusters
Resolution Parameter controlling how many clusters you get
Pseudobulk Summing counts per donor × cell type before testing
Differential abundance Testing whether cell-type proportions changed
Compositional data Proportions that must sum to 1, so they cannot move independently
